learn: Why LLMs need external knowledge, and why retraining isn't the answer
Semantic search and the retrieve → augment → generate flow
Selecting context: top-K vs thresholding, and re-ranking
Token budgets and why long chats degrade
Chunking: size, overlap, stride and chunk counts
Evaluating retrieval with precision and recall against a golden set

intro.why: Retrieval-augmented generation is how most real LLM applications use private, current and verifiable knowledge. Its engineering is mostly arithmetic and trade-offs (budgets, chunking, precision vs recall, graph vs vector), which this session works through with numbers.

true positives, false positives, false negatives

sections.title: LLM limits and why RAG
sections.plain: Give a brilliant but out-of-date model the right pages to read at question time.
sections.body:
An LLM is like a brilliant scholar locked in a windowless room since a cut-off date. Limits: knowledge cut-off and no real-time data; no private knowledge (your HR policies, code, databases); hallucination; long-context degradation (long chats get compacted and drift); privacy and black-box concerns (where is my data processed?); and no continual learning.

Retraining daily is impractical (huge compute, days to months per version); even parameter-efficient fine-tuning (e.g. low-rank adaptation) is too heavy to rerun whenever a policy document changes, and it's a poor way to add facts.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation: retrieve relevant information from an external knowledge base, augment the prompt with it, and generate the answer from it. It turns a closed-book exam into an open-book exam: find the right pages, put them on the desk, answer from them.

sections.title: Semantic search and the RAG flow
sections.plain: Embed the question, find the most similar chunks, paste them into the prompt, and let the model answer from them.
sections.body:
Keyword search misses "pricing for computer hardware fixes" for the query "cost of laptop repair". Semantic search embeds the query and every knowledge-base chunk into vectors and returns the chunks with the highest cosine (or dot-product) similarity, matching meaning even when words differ.

  1. User query: "Can I sit the final exam if my attendance is 70%?"
  2. Embed the query; search the vector database of chunked documents (attendance, exam, hostel, fee policies).
  3. Retrieve the top chunks: the two attendance paragraphs, not whole documents and not the hostel rules.
  4. Augment the prompt: instructions + retrieved chunks + question.
  5. The LLM generates a grounded answer (and can cite the chunks).

A RAG system has two jobs and its quality is the product of both: retrieve well (the right chunks) and answer well (use them faithfully).

sections.title: Top-K vs thresholding and re-ranking
sections.plain: Keep a fixed number of best chunks, or every chunk above a quality bar; re-order candidates before cutting.
sections.body:
Top-K ranking keeps the K highest-scoring chunks regardless of how good they are. Thresholding keeps all chunks scoring above τ (e.g. 0.80), whether that's 3 or 300. With scores 0.94, 0.88, 0.81, 0.74, 0.69, … both pick the same three chunks, but they are different rules: thresholding adapts to quality (a good default), top-K guarantees a fixed budget.

  • Too many chunks (a permissive threshold over a huge corpus): the context window fills, compaction kicks in, and noise dilutes or derails the answer.
  • Too few (hard top-3 when ten chunks matter, or all scores mediocre at 0.5–0.7): the model lacks information.

Re-ranking: when the best 20 scores differ only in the third decimal (0.990, 0.991, 0.9903…), a hard top-10 cut may drop chunk 11, which held the answer. Retrieval was fine; ranking did the damage. A second, more accurate model (e.g. a cross-encoder) re-orders candidates before the final cut.

sections.title: The token budget
sections.plain: Subtract the fixed parts of the prompt from the window; only the rest is for retrieved chunks.
sections.body:
$$\text{Available} = \text{MaxContext} - (\text{SystemPrompt} + \text{UserQuery}),\qquad \#\text{chunks} = \Big\lfloor\frac{\text{Available}}{\text{ChunkSize}}\Big\rfloor$$

Example 1: 10,000 − (300 + 200) = 9,500 tokens. Example 2: 8,192 − (300 + 220) = 7,672; with 512-token chunks, ⌊7,672/512⌋ = 14 chunks (a 15th would overflow, so round down). The model's own reasoning and answer also need room, so practical systems reserve output tokens too.

The subtraction runs every turn: conversation history keeps consuming the window. Past roughly 80–90% usage, systems compact (summarise) older turns; compaction is lossy, so after many multi-turn steps the original context is gone and answers drift: long chats degrade by arithmetic, not mystery.

sections.title: Chunking: size, overlap and stride
sections.plain: Split documents into overlapping pieces so ideas at the boundaries survive.
sections.body:
A 500-page book (~1 million tokens) can't go into the prompt whole, so documents are split into chunks (say 500 tokens) and only relevant chunks are retrieved. Clean cuts can split a sentence or idea in half; overlap repeats the tail of each chunk at the start of the next. With chunk size 6 and overlap 2: chunk 1 = A B C D E F, chunk 2 = E F G H I J (E F shared).

$$\text{Stride} = \text{ChunkSize} - \text{Overlap},\qquad \#\text{chunks} = \Big\lceil\frac{\text{DocumentTokens}}{\text{Stride}}\Big\rceil$$

Worked: 18,200 tokens, size 600, overlap 120 → stride 480 → ⌈18,200/480⌉ = ⌈37.9⌉ = 38 chunks. Ceiling because the final partial window still becomes a (shorter) chunk; contrast with the token budget's floor. Rule: floor for how many fit inside a limit, ceiling for how many pieces cover everything.

Trade-offs: small chunks are precise but lose context; large chunks carry context but dilute similarity and eat the budget; more overlap improves continuity at the cost of storage. Splitting on natural boundaries (headings, paragraphs) often beats fixed token windows.

sections.title: Retrieval precision and recall
sections.plain: Precision: how much of what you fetched was useful. Recall: how much of what was useful you fetched.
sections.body:
Evaluate the retriever against a golden set: for each test question, humans list the chunks that should be retrieved. Each chunk is then a TP (relevant, fetched), FP (irrelevant, fetched), FN (relevant, missed) or TN.

$$P = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} = \frac{\text{relevant retrieved}}{\text{retrieved}},\qquad R = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} = \frac{\text{relevant retrieved}}{\text{relevant}}$$
  • 2 relevant chunks; system retrieves 5 including both: P = 0.4 (noisy), R = 1.0.
  • 1,000 retrieved, 10 relevant: P = 0.01: technically the answer is there, drowned in noise.
  • 20 relevant exist, 13 retrieved: R = 0.65: the answer can only be 65% complete.

Generation quality is bounded by retrieval quality (garbage in, garbage out). Loose thresholds raise recall and cut precision (noise, token burn); tight top-K does the opposite. End-to-end evaluation also checks faithfulness (is the answer supported by the retrieved text?) and answer relevance.

sections.title: The latency budget
sections.plain: Add up the time of every stage and check what still fits.
sections.body:
$$\text{Total latency} = \text{Embedding} + \text{Retrieval} + (\text{Re-ranking}) + \text{Generation}$$

Worked: allowed 2,500 ms; embedding 150, retrieval 420, generation 1,600 → used 2,170, remaining 330 ms. A 300 ms re-ranker fits; a 400 ms one doesn't unless another stage gets faster.

Levers: cache query and document embeddings, use approximate nearest-neighbour indexes, limit candidate counts before re-ranking, use smaller or distilled re-rankers, stream generation, and shorten prompts (fewer, better chunks also reduce generation time and cost).

sections.title: Graph RAG and when graphs beat vectors
sections.plain: Retrieve by walking a knowledge graph when the answer is a relationship.
sections.body:
Recall: ontology (rules) + data (specifics) = knowledge graph (M12), like a map platform's structure (roads connect cities) plus data (specific roads and hospitals). In Graph RAG, the system identifies entities in the query (often by vector search over node embeddings), traverses edges 1–2 hops out, and gives the connected facts and documents to the LLM.

Decision rule: if the question touches one entity and its immediate facts ("which course is Rahul enrolled in?"), vector search already finds it and a graph adds hops for nothing. Graphs win when information is highly connected and the connection is the answer: "how are Rahul and Dr. Vidhi related?" → Rahul → enrolled in → NLP ← teaches ← Dr. Vidhi, a path no single text chunk states.

vector RAGGraph RAG
dataunstructured chunksnodes and edges
retrievaldense similarity searchtraversal / graph queries (Cypher)
reasoningmostly single-hopmulti-hop
explainabilitylowhigh (visible paths)
integration effortmoderatehigh
best forgeneral Q&A over documentsconnected, domain-specific logic

Many systems store knowledge in both and route each query.

sections.title: KG–LLM synergy and applications
sections.plain: Graphs supply verified, connected facts; LLMs supply language; each can build or use the other.
sections.body:
1. KG-enhanced LLMs (retrieval): the LLM consults the graph: Obama → born in → Honolulu → located in → USA answers "which country?" without guessing.
  2. LLM-augmented KGs (extraction): an LLM reads text ("EGF up-regulates miR-31") and adds the triple (EGF, upregulates, miR-31) to a graph database.
  3. Synergised: continuous loops of representation learning and neuro-symbolic reasoning (search engines, dialogue systems).

Applications: hospital graphs (patients, doctors, departments, diseases, procedures) where community detection may surface unexplored disease links; blast radius in cloud infrastructure (a data centre fails → traverse to every affected pod, customer and service, pure multi-hop traversal); routing incident reports to the right department; personalised medicine with biomedical KGs; and explainable AI in medicine, finance and defence, where a visible reasoning path answers "why did you say that?". Research directions include joint text–KG pre-training and graph-neural-network retrieval.

sections.title: Multimodal and agentic RAG
sections.plain: Retrieve from images, tables and video too; and let an agent loop through plan, retrieve and reason until it has enough.
sections.body:
Multimodal RAG: much knowledge lives in images, charts, tables, video and audio. "What was the company's Q3 revenue?" may be answerable only from a chart in the annual report. Multimodal embedding models map different data types into a shared space (a dog photo near the word "dog"), so text queries retrieve images and tables, and a multimodal LLM reads them. A cheaper route: narrate every modality to text (describe images and tables, transcribe video) and run ordinary text RAG, accepting some loss of fidelity.

Agentic RAG: standard RAG is one linear pass. "Compare the annual energy output of nuclear vs solar in 2024" needs several retrievals: plan sub-goals → retrieve (cache results) → reason (extract numbers, check units, compare) → notice something is missing (solar) → loop → answer with citations. Multi-agent systems add sub-agents with declared skills and retrieval limits.

Caution: agents inherit LLM flaws; they "fail politely", agreeing they were wrong even when they weren't. Observability and evaluation of every step (RAG-specific metrics frameworks exist) matter as much as the pipeline design. The durable fundamentals: budgets, chunking, precision/recall and the graph-vs-vector rule.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Hybrid retrieval: combining keyword (BM25) and dense scores often beats either alone, especially for names and codes.
  • Lost in the middle: models use information at the start and end of long contexts better than the middle; order retrieved chunks accordingly.
  • RAG vs fine-tuning: RAG for facts that change or must be cited; fine-tuning for style, format and behaviour.
  • Security: retrieved documents can contain prompt injections; treat them as data, not instructions.

code.title: RAG arithmetic
code.explain: Computes the token budgets (9,500; 7,672 → 14 chunks), stride and chunk count (480 → 38), shows overlapped chunks of A…J, compares top-K with a 0.80 threshold on strong and mediocre score profiles, works the three precision/recall examples and checks whether 300 ms and 400 ms re-rankers fit the latency budget.
mistakes: Using ceiling for the token budget or floor for the chunk count.
Forgetting the system prompt in the budget.
code.notes: The ceiling formula counts every start position, so the last chunk may be short.
code.code:
"""RAG arithmetic: token budget, chunk stride/count, overlap chunking, top-K vs threshold,
retrieval precision/recall, and latency budget."""
import math

def available(max_ctx, sys_prompt, query): return max_ctx - (sys_prompt + query)
a1 = available(10_000, 300, 200); a2 = available(8_192, 300, 220)
print(f"available tokens: {a1}; {a2} -> {a2 // 512} chunks of 512 fit (floor)")

def n_chunks(doc, size, overlap):
    stride = size - overlap
    return stride, math.ceil(doc / stride)
s, n = n_chunks(18_200, 600, 120)
print(f"stride = {s}, chunks = ceil(18200/{s}) = ceil({18200/s:.2f}) = {n}")

def chunk(tokens, size, overlap):
    stride = size - overlap
    return [tokens[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(tokens), stride) if tokens[i:i + size]]
print("overlap demo:", ["".join(c) for c in chunk(list("ABCDEFGHIJ"), 6, 2)])

scores = {"C1": .94, "C2": .88, "C3": .81, "C4": .74, "C5": .69, "C6": .62, "C7": .55, "C8": .41, "C9": .30, "C10": .11}
topk = sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)[:3]
thr = [c for c, v in scores.items() if v >= 0.80]
print("top-3:", topk, "| threshold 0.80:", thr)
weak = {f"C{i}": v for i, v in enumerate([.62, .58, .55, .51, .50], 1)}
print("mediocre scores -> top-3:", sorted(weak, key=weak.get, reverse=True)[:3], "| threshold 0.80:", [c for c, v in weak.items() if v >= .8])

def pr(tp, retrieved, relevant): return tp / retrieved, tp / relevant
print("precision/recall examples:", pr(2, 5, 2), pr(10, 1000, 10), (None, 13 / 20))

budget, used = 2500, 150 + 420 + 1600
print(f"latency used {used} ms, remaining {budget - used} ms -> 300 ms re-ranker fits: {300 <= budget - used}; 400 ms: {400 <= budget - used}")

code.title: A mini retriever and Graph RAG traversal
code.explain: Ranks policy chunks for the attendance question with TF-IDF cosine (a stand-in for dense embeddings), measures precision/recall at K = 1, 2, 3 against a golden set, builds an augmented prompt, then answers a relationship question (Rahul → NLP ← Dr. Vidhi) and a blast-radius question by graph traversal.
mistakes: Evaluating retrieval without a golden set.
Using vector search for multi-hop relationship questions.
code.notes: Real systems use dense embeddings and a vector database.
code.code:
"""A tiny retrieval pipeline (TF-IDF), why ranking cut-offs matter, and when graph traversal beats vectors."""
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity
import networkx as nx

chunks = {
    "attendance#1": "Students need at least 75 percent attendance in a course to be eligible for the final exam.",
    "attendance#2": "Attendance between 65 and 75 percent may be condoned on medical grounds with documents.",
    "exam#1": "Final exams are held in the last two weeks of the term; admit cards are issued online.",
    "hostel#1": "Hostel residents must return by 10 pm and register visitors at the gate.",
    "fees#1": "Tuition fees are payable in two instalments; late payment attracts a fine.",
}
q = "Can I sit the final exam if my attendance is 70 percent?"
vec = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english").fit(list(chunks.values()) + [q])
sims = cosine_similarity(vec.transform([q]), vec.transform(list(chunks.values())))[0]
ranked = sorted(zip(chunks, sims), key=lambda x: -x[1])
for k, s in ranked: print(f"  {s:.3f}  {k}")
gold = {"attendance#1", "attendance#2"}
for K in (1, 2, 3):
    got = {k for k, _ in ranked[:K]}
    tp = len(got & gold)
    print(f"top-{K}: precision {tp/K:.2f}, recall {tp/len(gold):.2f}")
prompt = "Answer only from the context.\n" + "\n".join(chunks[k] for k, _ in ranked[:2]) + f"\nQuestion: {q}"
print("augmented prompt length (words):", len(prompt.split()))

# Graph RAG: a relationship question that no single chunk answers
G = nx.DiGraph()
G.add_edge("Rahul", "NLP", rel="enrolled_in"); G.add_edge("Dr. Vidhi", "NLP", rel="teaches")
G.add_edge("Dr. Vidhi", "CS Department", rel="works_in"); G.add_edge("NLP", "CS Department", rel="offered_by")
U = G.to_undirected()
path = nx.shortest_path(U, "Rahul", "Dr. Vidhi")
print("How are Rahul and Dr. Vidhi related? path:", " -> ".join(path),
      "| edges:", [G.edges[a, b]["rel"] if G.has_edge(a, b) else G.edges[b, a]["rel"] for a, b in zip(path, path[1:])])

# Blast radius: everything downstream of a failed data centre
B = nx.DiGraph([("DC-1", "pod-a"), ("DC-1", "pod-b"), ("DC-2", "pod-c"), ("pod-a", "customer-X"), ("pod-b", "customer-Y"),
                ("pod-b", "billing-service"), ("pod-c", "customer-Z")])
print("blast radius of DC-1:", sorted(nx.descendants(B, "DC-1")))
